startup.name: e2e
startup.one_liner: the software verification layer for the agentic coding era
startup.description: e2e is an eight person team based in Warsaw and remote, positioned as the software verification layer for the agentic coding era. The input gives only the one liner, so the product is inferred: tooling that automatically checks that code written by AI agents works, most likely end to end tests and checks run in CI. Buyers are engineering teams shipping a lot of agent written code. No description, traction or customers are given.

yc_acceptance.basis: Starting rate about 1 percent (YC investor line, third party range 0.6 to 2 percent). Test setup: already accepted, so this is a reference only. Up for a team of 8 in a topical category the agentic coding wave created, and for a clear painful problem. Down for a thin description and a crowded testing field. Net about 5 percent as a plain applicant.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly pass because the pitch is a category label with no stated wedge or customer. AI testing and verification for coding agents already had funded startups, and a reviewer would ask what e2e does that Momentic, QA Wolf or the coding agents themselves do not. Without early usage or a named user pain, the application reads as timely but undifferentiated.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Anchor 51 percent, ours 72 percent. A hot category in spring 2026 with a team of 8 raises odds, within 1.5x of the anchor. The definition here is a round above about 500K within 12 months, which is looser than the anchor's any seed round.

bands.rationale: Typical 2022+ B2B seed: median 3.2M, p25 2.0M, p75 5.0M (base_rates B2B 2022-2025). A team of 8 has a larger burn, so a normal seed is the single likeliest outcome.
Strong developer tools seeds in the AI coding wave are priced richer, near the p75 of 5M and above.
Small round from angels and YC follow on, or a bridge. Thin band.
Upside: a breakout open source or viral developer adoption pulls a large seed.

ladder.why_it_fails: It does not clear a round above about 500K in 12 months if investors see it as one more AI testing tool. Rainforest took three years from batch to a Series A, and recent entrants like Autosana raised only a 3.2M seed about 9 months after the batch. Without paying customers and a clear reason to pick e2e over Momentic or the coding agents' own checks, investors in a crowded field pass, and the team of 8 burns the YC money quickly.

ladder.why_it_fails: A seed round is raised on promise, a Series A on revenue. Reflect and Rainforest show that testing tools can stall at seed or take years to reach A, and Reflect was sold to SmartBear after a 1.8M seed. e2e needs several repeat paying teams, and the risk is that coding agents and CI platforms bundle verification, so growth flattens below the roughly 1M to 2M annual revenue an A investor expects.

ladder.why_it_fails: Reaching a Series B needs a durable product moat and rising revenue. Testing has been a hard category to grow past the 40M raised by Rainforest, and buyers can switch. The model labs and platform vendors keep adding verification, so e2e must become a system of record that engineering teams cannot drop, or growth slows and the B round never materializes.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series C needs a large, scaled business. The testing category has few outcomes of that size, and a standalone verification vendor would face the largest platform vendors. Few B2B companies in the cohort get there, and most that stay independent grow slowly with revenue instead of raising again.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most likely the company stalls because it is one of many AI testing startups with similar pitches and no unique data or distribution. Reflect ended in an acquisition by an established tester, and several 2025 and 2026 batch entries target the same job. The coding agent vendors can add verification as a feature, which caps a standalone category and leads to acquihires or a slow bootstrapped path.

killers.risk: Coding agent vendors bundle verification and make a standalone layer unnecessary
killers.evidence: Agent vendors can run tests inside their own loop at no marginal cost and own the developer relationship.
killers.mitigation: Stay vendor neutral and become the shared check across several agents and CI systems.

killers.risk: Crowded AI testing field with many similar pitches and funded rivals
killers.evidence: Autosana, Lark, Narrative and Momentic all pitch AI end to end testing for teams shipping AI written code.
killers.mitigation: Pick a narrow, painful wedge such as one stack or one failure type and win a few paying teams fast.

killers.risk: Trust and accuracy: flaky or wrong verdicts make teams turn the tool off
killers.evidence: Testing tools live or die on false positives; Rainforest moved toward no code automation after crowd testing proved unreliable.
killers.mitigation: Publish precision numbers and keep humans in the loop for the first customers.

killers.risk: Unclear buyer and slow budget: developers use it free, nobody pays
killers.evidence: Developer tools often get usage without budget, as with several open source tooling companies in the cohort.
killers.mitigation: Charge per run or per repo from day one.

technical_complexity.rationale: Running and judging end to end tests across many stacks is a solid engineering job a small team can build in three months, but reliable verdicts on agent written code, low flakiness and fast infrastructure are hard to make excellent. Depends on model quality and CI integrations.

takeover_risk.rationale: A well resourced rival could add basic verification in under a year and has distribution through the developer workflow. Incentive is strong because verification keeps users inside their product. Past testing companies like Reflect ended up inside larger vendors.

evidence.claim: Seed funding in AI testing and QA has been active, with an aggregator tracking about 30 startups.
Competing startups such as Autosana and Momentic raised seed rounds to sell agentic QA.

roadmap.goal: A clear wedge and a few real users of the verification product.
actions: Choose one stack and one failure type and ship a working verifier on it.
Get three engineering teams using it on agent written pull requests.

roadmap.goal: Paying customers and visible usage that justify a round above 500K.
actions: Charge per repo or per run and sign five paying teams.
Publish precision and false positive numbers and open source a core piece to build trust.
roadmap.proof: Recurring revenue and a public accuracy benchmark.

roadmap.goal: Repeatable revenue from teams that did not know the founders.
actions: Hire a first sales and customer success owner and add CI integrations.
Show net revenue retention and a pipeline of larger teams.
roadmap.proof: About 1M to 2M in annual recurring revenue with strong retention.

roadmap.goal: A category position that agent vendors cannot copy.
actions: Build cross vendor integrations and enterprise controls.
Collect data on failures that improves the verifier.

pros.evidence: Agent written code increases the need to verify it, and funded peers show investors will back the space.
Eight people at batch start is larger than the usual two person YC team, giving more build capacity.

strengths: Very short and tells developers what the product does
weaknesses: Generic abbreviation that is hard to search for and trademark
Shared with the testing term, so no distinct identity
brand.rationale: A name that is the category term gives instant meaning to developers but no brand ownership, like past YC names that were descriptive and hard to search. Brand is secondary here and mostly neutral, so it does not move the ladder.

narrative.headline: A timely but crowded bet on verifying agent written code; likely to raise a seed and then face a hard Series A.
narrative.general_summary: e2e sells the verification layer for agentic coding, which is a real and growing need as teams ship code written by AI. The same insight is shared by several funded startups, and the YC record shows testing companies tend to raise a seed and then struggle to scale, as Rainforest and Reflect did. The team of 8 gives it build capacity, and the timing helps a seed above 500K within a year. The path to a Series A depends on paying teams and a wedge that coding agents and CI platforms cannot bundle away. The description is thin, so uncertainty is wide.
